title: Why to Not Not Start a Startup: dismantling the 16 reasons founders hesitate
summary: Paul Graham lists the reasons people hesitate to start startups and says which are real and which are bogus. Most are bogus: youth, inexperience, intelligence, business knowledge and no idea matter little. The real ones are no cofounder and a family to support. The essay also argues for making something people love first and worrying about revenue later.

principles.text: Don't worry about business knowledge at first. Build something people want, and money follows.
principles.quote: All you need to know in this phase is how to build things people want. If you succeed, you'll have to think about how to make money from it. But this is so easy you can pick it up on the fly.

principles.text: If users love you, you can always make money from that. If they don't, a clever business model won't save you.
principles.quote: if users love you, you can always make money from that somehow, and if they don't, the cleverest business model in the world won't save you.

principles.text: The most valuable truths are the ones most people don't believe. Push toward ideas you know are good that others reject.
principles.quote: The most valuable truths are the ones most people don't believe. They're like undervalued stocks. If you start with them, you'll have the whole field to yourself.

principles.text: Get a cofounder before anything else. A startup is too much for one person, and investors prefer teams.
principles.quote: Not having a cofounder is a real problem. A startup is too much for one person to bear.

principles.text: Determination is probably the single best predictor of founder success. Many founders underestimate how much of it they have.
principles.quote: You need a lot of determination to succeed as a startup founder. It's probably the single best predictor of success.

principles.text: Find startup ideas by supplying something missing in your own life, even if it seems narrow.
principles.quote: A need that's narrow but genuine is a better starting point than one that's broad but hypothetical.
